passage:
The plotter jammed at 6:10 pm, twenty minutes before the municipal submission, and Swati simply sat down on the print-room floor of the architecture firm.
She didn't decide to cry. It just came, heavy and shaking, the kind she couldn't stop by breathing.
Yogesh, her team lead, found her there. He crouched a little distance away. "I'll email the drawings myself. You're going home."
"I can do it," she said, and couldn't even stand.
In the cab she stared at her hands. Three years without missing a deadline, and now this. Pathetic, she thought.
At home she slept fourteen hours without waking. The next morning her body felt like wet sand.
Yogesh had messaged: "Submission went through. Take tomorrow off. Let's talk on Thursday about your load, no pressure."
She read it twice and felt ashamed and, underneath that, strangely grateful.

qa.q: How long did Swati sleep after she got home?
qa.a: She slept fourteen hours without waking.

qa.q: What did Swati think of herself in the cab, and why?
qa.a: She thought she was pathetic, because after three years without missing a deadline, breaking down felt like failure.

qa.q: What turning point does Yogesh's message open for Swati?
qa.a: It lets her rest properly and then talk honestly on Thursday about her load, treating the crash as a signal rather than a failure.

qa.q: What might Yogesh have felt finding Swati on the print-room floor?
qa.a: He may have been shaken to see a reliable team member unable to stand, and chose to take the task off her and send her home instead of pushing the deadline.

grounding: Shows a young professional breaking down before a deadline and sleeping fourteen hours, a crash that feels like failure but is the body forcing rest.

passage:
Thomas,
I'm writing this from bed at 3 pm on a Monday. The quarterly deck was due at ten. I set four alarms. I heard every one of them, and I could not make my body get up. Not lazy-couldn't. Couldn't, like my arms were filled with sand.
At eleven I finally messaged my manager: "Unwell, can't make it today." Then I cried for an hour, because I have never, ever done that.
It feels like I've failed at the one thing I'm known for. You know me, the 2 am edits person.
But lying here I keep thinking how I've been saying "I'll rest after this project" since March. Maybe my body just stopped waiting for me to agree.
I'm scared of what I'll say to my manager tomorrow.
Can you call me tonight?
Noor

qa.q: How many alarms did Noor set?
Why does Noor feel like a failure after missing the deadline?
qa.a: Noor is upset because Noor is known for 2 am edits and has never missed work like this, so staying in bed feels like failing at the one thing Noor is known for.

qa.q: What could Noor do before facing the manager tomorrow?
qa.a: Noor could rest today, talk it through with Thomas tonight and plan to be honest about months of overwork; if the heavy tiredness keeps going, a doctor visit would help.

qa.q: What might Thomas feel when this letter arrives?
qa.a: Thomas may be worried to hear that a friend who never misses deadlines couldn't get out of bed, and glad to be the one Noor reached out to.

grounding: Illustrates being unable to get out of bed for a Monday deadline, feeling it as failure while sensing the body has enforced overdue rest.
